Here are some reflections about the usage of AI for writing. Instinctively, it does make sense to think about how humans should write their own text. The main benefit is that you will become the complete owner of the product that is being presented. Nonetheless, as we have discussed with other colleagues many times, we do need some help trying to organize our ideas. The way that I've been using AI for writing is mostly around providing a stream of thought with the things that I would like to include in my text. I usually go paragraph by paragraph, trying to craft the content without asking the AI to incorporate additional things into it. 

## The research assistant

One example that I've been thinking of recently is a research assistant. Research assistants usually take on the task of writing code for you, conducting experiments for you, and even writing itself. But many times, just as we do as humans, as any other person, they will make mistakes. But because of that, the argument is that the AI is imperfect; it's flawed, because the same work that humans tend to do is also flawed. Furthermore, when it comes to coding and things that have a way to rationalize a thought process, AI has been remarkably good. With the incorporation of model context protocols and other tools that allow AIs to validate their products, it is becoming extremely good at writing code and math. The argument of hallucinations and the things maybe not working properly has less weight these days. 

Now, at the same time, it is very easy to feel lost when you see text that was written by the AI, and you don't comprehend it. But that is the key part, the part that makes you own the generated text or product. If you are not critical about the things that the AI writes for you, just like if you were not critical of the things that your colleagues or research assistants write for you, then you'll be committing the same mistake as if you were a person. The fact that this is not a person is somewhat irrelevant here. You wouldn't accept submitting a paper if you haven't checked it. Putting your name, branding, things without you checking the validity of it or at least reviewing it is bad practice overall, not just for AI. 

My experience writing with AI has been a bit different from what it is today. Since I started working with Grammarly about five years ago now, my writing skills have been going up significantly. I can tell this just from my own experience and from discussing and presenting my text with other colleagues.

The reason for that is that most of the time the way that I write is the following: I will write something, present it raw, and the AI will make corrections on it. In other words the AI is not writing the text for me; it's just correcting what I wrote. That is the fundamental difference, I think, with what other people are doing these days: they are asking the AI to just write something for them without specifying what the content is explicitly or what details need to be around it. This makes me think that we should have a set of rules, or at least a procedure, when it comes to teaching people how to use AI. In it we tell them what the best way of using AI is while at the same time owning what comes out of it. 

Another important thing to think about is the abstraction layers as we do in computer science. The way that other programmers have presented this is AI as another abstraction layer. You don't see anyone writing their own assembly code these days. It's mostly using C, C++, or another higher-level programming language. So then why don't we think about AI in similar terms? A scientist may argue that if the AI writes it for you, it is not of your authorship, but somebody can say something similar with coding or even going backward. Thinking about the printer, probably when the printer came out many people was against it because you have a machine doing the work that you will do by hand. Here is something similar but the main difference is that the AI can at some level create on your behalf. So then the main difference is or a key component is how much freedom in a sense do you give the AI to do things on your behalf? And at the same time, how much importance do you give to every single thing that the AI does for you? If we star micromanaging everything that the AI age and task for us, that's a problem.


## Why not using AI for writing?

Now let's think about arguments against and for using AI for writing. More specifically something in favor is that it can significantly improve your clarity and grammar if you are passing your own text. This also reduces the time spent trying to polish the text. Now somebody can say that polishing the text is an experience in itself and also part of the process. Against that I don't have any particular argument other than saying that you can still learn from the process of seeing how the AI has improved your writing. Sure it is weaker but also it depends on which part of the output you value more. From a productivity standpoint, for sure, using the AI will accelerate things if you use it properly. You can get a higher throughput with less effort but it can also negatively affect the learning process. Nevertheless this is assuming that you have a single interaction with the AI so you'll see this a single time. Yet unconsciously I believe that, the same way that you learn to write better when you have interactions with people, the same will happen with AI because our brains are wired that way. If you start making the same mistake over and over and you realize that the AI is correcting that over and over again, you will tend to make that error less frequently (which is what happened to me when it came to Grammarly). 

Now what is the problem with people using AI for writing? Let's take a look at it in the two extremes. If somebody ask an AR to write an entire paper for them. Of course they are not the authors of that paper because none of their ideas is actually reflected in it. They did not spend any time analyzing the data so the conclusions did not came from their analysis. No time to sign in it and no time reflecting about what are the repercussions of their results. Now a lot of this may sound like naive, but I think ultimately the issue is about accountability. If the analysis of the AI did is incorrect than the author, the responsible person is the one who is accountable because a machine cannot be accountable for it and that's where the penalty can come. If you polish a study that presents the wrong conclusions, then you should be panalyzed if you didn't went through it regularly and the same happens for the reviewers involved in the process. It might be that AI was involved in writing it but if not even the reviewers called the issues then there is a problem. At the same time with the pays at which we are writing papers, it is harder and harder to be able to review them properly which is where AI can come into the game. Just like I've used AI for helping me writing, I don't see a bad point in asking AI review on a paper for you highlighting things on your behalf. The question now is will the things that the AI will highlight are appropriate for you or our paperwork said or not?. So the main question, it seems that is who is responsible for it? Because if I have a paper in which a person made a mistake, how do we penalize stas versus somebody writing a paper using AI? Do we penalize it differently? The implications are actually the same. Both are an error so then that might be a bright type of hypothesis or situation to place is in assume that we have the same type of error, but one was made by the AI and the other one was made by a human. What's the accountability that we expect from each situation? Is it different? 

On The other extreme somebody not using AI for writing at all. It's not bad. The main issue there is the productivity level. If you're not using AI, you will spend more time polishing and adjusting the text for sure. That may improve you as a scientist for the future, but then how important is that gain? Ultimately, when you can have an AI doing that for you now this is under the assumption that whenever the AI is writing something for you or on your behalf, you understand what it is writing for you because if you don't use it as an assistant, but rather you just use it to do the task for you replacing you entirely, then that's the main issue, isn't it?

## The Incentives

Somebody else can say that the matter practice of allowing people to use AI for writing things should be socially penalized or rejected just like we reject plagiarism. The problem with that argument is that it's not the same thing when it comes about incentives and policing. We don't do plagiarism because of two things. First, if we get caught, we are penalized by society and second there is a high chance of getting caught. In the case of using AI for writing; neither is true today. We don't have currently any system that allows us to easily identify cases in which AI has been heavily used for writing and even if we identify that the current penalties are not clear at the society level or even the scientific level as the community is polarized. 

Ultimately, I think that we should be working towards a solution that is more embracing of AI. There's no way that the models are going to be getting any worse. On the contrary, they are getting better and better every time. And if we as scholars start to close ourselves toward the rest of the world and how we use, AI is not going to be good for the community, the science or the students. Students going to the job market without having a proper AI training or using AI at the level of people in industry are going to be penalized. 


## Misc

Now I think that my case may be a bit different because I am self-conscious about the importance of owning the words that you write or you share. Yet it is impossible to set aside the appeal of having an assistant that can write for you, transmitting ideas to paper in a way that is clear for others to read.
